summary: A response to RFC 346 on satellite delays, from John Davidson at the University of Hawaii, which was due to join the ARPANET by satellite. He describes how the BCC 500 research group there was studying buffer allocation and partitioned echoing as ways to cope with long delays. It builds on design ideas from the BCC 500 communication system.

plainLanguage.summary: A school across the ocean knows its messages will take a long trip through space, so it explains how it is planning its computers to feel less slow.

questions: how to handle long network delays
subtitle: Solutions for handling long communication delays from satellite connections.

tldr.problem: The University of Hawaii was about to join the ARPANET via satellite link, which introduces multi-second transmission delays that make interactive computing feel sluggish and require careful buffer management.
tldr.mechanism: Hawaii's BCC 500 research group adapted concepts from their earlier distributed communication system, including partitioned echoing where local concentrators provide immediate echo feedback to terminals while coordinating with the remote host.
tldr.outcome: The work explored how to make interactive sessions tolerable over long-delay links and discussed whether such solutions could be incorporated into TIPs and IMPs network-wide.

today: RFC 355 documents Hawaii's early research on satellite networking challenges. Though marked as Unknown status, it is an important historical record of how the ARPANET community tackled the problem of interactive computing over long-delay links, work that would become relevant again decades later with satellite internet services.

sections.title: The Satellite Delay Problem
sections.content:
RFC 355 is a response to RFC 346, which discussed satellite communication delays on the ARPANET. The University of Hawaii was preparing to join the network via satellite, which introduces delays of several seconds for round-trip communication—far longer than the millisecond delays of terrestrial links.

For interactive computing, such delays are a serious usability problem. When a user types a character, they expect immediate feedback (an echo) on their terminal. With a satellite link, they would see a delay of seconds between typing and feedback. The BCC 500 research group at Hawaii had been studying solutions to this problem, drawing on their experience with a distributed communication system that served geographically scattered users.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages sent through space satellites take a long time to go up and come back down. Users waiting for an echo of what they type will feel very frustrated, so Hawaii's team thought hard about solutions.

sections.title: Partitioned Echoing and Buffer Allocation
sections.content:
The BCC 500 system, designed to serve users at remote concentrators accessing a central computer, implemented partitioned echoing. Local terminals get echo feedback from a character input/output microprocessor (CHIO) at the concentrator, making the echo appear instantaneous to the user. Meanwhile, the actual processing happens at the central CPU, which communicates asynchronously with the concentrator.

For the ARPANET, this approach means a local Telnet or TIP at Hawaii could provide immediate echo, while actual data flows to and from mainland hosts over the satellite link. The challenge is coordinating between local echoing and remote processing to avoid duplicates, garbled output, or lost commands.

The BCC 500 solved this coordination at the concentrator and CPU level, but extending the approach to the asynchronous message-based ARPANET, especially with satellite delays, requires new thinking. Hawaii was also coordinating with the ILLIAC group at NASA-AMES on how to handle differences in terminal control conventions across different systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of waiting for an echo from far away, the local computer echoes immediately, then sends the real command later. It's like talking to a friend through a very slow echo chamber—you hear yourself right away, then later get the answer.

sections.title: Open Questions
sections.content:
The response raises important architectural questions. Could partitioned echoing be a function of User TELNETs or the TIP itself, rather than a special feature of Hawaii's system? Could it even be incorporated into the IMP layer so all systems could benefit? If so, how would it interact with existing concentrator systems like the BCC 500 that already do local echoing?

Different hosts use different terminal control conventions, and resolving conflicts between these systems is another challenge. Davidson invited feedback from the ARPANET community and expressed willingness to share Hawaii's research findings with other sites and coordinate with research groups like ILLIAC on solving these broader networking problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Hawaii asked big questions: Should every computer do this? Can the network itself help? How do we make sure different computers all play nicely together?
